title: Build an attack path from prerequisites
mechanism: An attack path links an entry point to a violated trust boundary and a useful capability. Discovery, access, privilege and impact are separate stages, not guaranteed steps.
prerequisites: State attacker position, reachable services, existing credentials, required victim behavior and intended effect. A local-link attacker has different opportunities from a remote internet client.
reasoning: For each transition, ask what the receiver trusts and what the attacker can actually control. Stop the proposed path wherever a prerequisite is missing instead of assuming success.
evidence: A reachable port or a diagram edge is not proof that the next stage is possible. Record known, inferred and untested conditions separately.
defense: Break the path with identity verification, scoped authorization, segmentation and monitoring. Retest the blocked transition and required legitimate behavior.

title: ARP spoofing and local-link interception
mechanism: ARP maps IPv4 neighbors to link-layer addresses on a local broadcast domain. A forged mapping can redirect a host traffic to an unintended peer if the host accepts it.
prerequisites: The attacker generally needs relevant local-link reachability or control of a component on that link. The target must accept an incorrect association and route useful traffic through it.
reasoning: Separate mapping manipulation, traffic forwarding and application compromise. Becoming a network intermediary does not automatically defeat correctly validated TLS. A broken forwarder may cause an outage instead of interception.
evidence: Inspect mapping changes, competing claims, switch-port identity and timing. Gateway failover or a legitimate replacement can also change the mapping.
defense: Use appropriate ARP inspection and trusted binding policies, secure switching access and end-to-end identity checks. Validate static-host exceptions and recovery paths.

title: Rogue DHCP and IPv6 router advertisements
mechanism: Configuration messages can influence address assignment, DNS settings and default routes. An unintended server or router can move traffic toward an untrusted path.
prerequisites: A receiver must accept the configuration message and use the resulting settings. IPv4 DHCP and IPv6 router discovery use different mechanisms and need separate review.
reasoning: Trace advertisement -> accepted configuration -> selected route or resolver -> subsequent connection. Check both address families; securing only IPv4 can leave an unexpected alternate path.
evidence: A rogue-looking announcement is not proof a client adopted it. Correlate the client configuration and traffic with trusted server/router inventory.
defense: Apply supported DHCP snooping and router-advertisement protections with correct trusted ports. Retest legitimate enrollment, redundancy and static configurations.

title: Name-resolution poisoning
mechanism: When a client cannot resolve a name through its intended mechanism, a fallback protocol may accept a response from an unintended peer. The redirected connection can expose a later authentication boundary.
prerequisites: The client must use the affected resolution path, accept the response and connect to a service of interest. Local protocols are not equivalent to poisoning every DNS resolver.
reasoning: Follow the unresolved name, competing responses, chosen address and subsequent connection. Separate redirection from credential disclosure or successful authentication relay.
evidence: Name-resolution packets alone do not establish that credentials were sent or a resource was accessed. Misconfigured legitimate software can generate similar queries.
defense: Remove unneeded fallback resolution, maintain reliable intended DNS, verify service identity and constrain authentication. Validate operational dependencies before disabling protocols.

title: Authentication relay versus replay
mechanism: Relay forwards a live authentication exchange to another service; replay reuses previously captured material. Challenge-response mechanisms can prevent simple replay yet remain vulnerable to relay in some deployments.
prerequisites: The target must accept the forwarded authentication in that context and grant a useful operation. Service binding, signing requirements and protocol-specific protections influence feasibility.
reasoning: Model who authenticates to whom, which identity the destination sees and what operation becomes available. Relay does not necessarily disclose the underlying password.
evidence: A captured authentication message is not proof of target acceptance. Required SMB signing protects SMB integrity; other protocols require their own binding and protection review.
defense: Require supported signing, channel/service binding or extended protections where appropriate, reduce legacy authentication and scope privileges. Validate the exact target protocol and deployment.

title: Password attacks and exposed credentials
mechanism: Online guessing, password spraying, credential stuffing and offline guessing use different inputs and produce different telemetry. Reused or exposed credentials may bypass the need to exploit a service.
prerequisites: Online testing needs an explicit account list, lockout knowledge and request budget. Credential validity, privilege and target reachability are separate prerequisites.
reasoning: Use synthetic authentication logs to compare many guesses against one account, one candidate across many accounts, and ordinary user mistakes. Evaluate the sequence and account impact.
evidence: A few failures do not prove an attack; a successful login does not identify the physical operator. Log coverage and clock alignment affect interpretation.
defense: Use strong authentication, MFA where supported, exposure response, appropriate rate controls and account monitoring. Test detection with approved synthetic events rather than real-user guessing.

title: VLAN and trunk trust failures
mechanism: VLANs separate Layer 2 domains when switch ports and trunks are correctly configured. Unexpected trunking or tagging behavior can undermine intended boundaries in some designs.
prerequisites: Feasibility depends on switch behavior, port configuration, native VLAN treatment and the specific topology. A generic VLAN-hopping claim is not valid for every switch.
reasoning: Review access versus trunk roles, negotiated behaviors and permitted VLAN lists. Identify the exact path a frame would take and whether a return path exists.
evidence: A tagged frame in a capture is not proof of crossing an unauthorized boundary. A routing rule can legitimately connect VLANs and must be assessed separately.
defense: Explicitly configure port roles, constrain trunks, isolate management and validate routing/firewall policy. Use a dedicated switch lab for any active tagging experiment.

title: Routing manipulation and source spoofing
mechanism: A forged source address changes a packet claim, not the sender actual return path. Routing manipulation changes where traffic travels and can affect availability or observation.
prerequisites: Source-spoofed exchanges often cannot receive replies without control of the path. Routing attacks depend on adjacency, policy or infrastructure compromise; local route changes and interdomain route leaks are different cases.
reasoning: Separate packet-origin validation, route acceptance and application identity. Inspect why an advertised route was accepted and whether it changed forwarding.
evidence: A route change can be legitimate failover. RPKI origin validation helps assess route origins but does not by itself validate every property of an entire path.
defense: Use appropriate source validation, authenticated control-plane relationships and route policy. Multihoming and asymmetric paths need careful validation to avoid blocking legitimate traffic.

title: DNS integrity, redirection and tunneling indicators
mechanism: Resolver compromise, unauthorized record changes and forged answers are distinct ways naming can misdirect clients. DNS can also carry unexpected data, but unusual names alone do not establish a covert channel.
prerequisites: Identify resolver trust, caching, authoritative control and whether the client validates the destination service identity. Determine which logs retain queries and responses.
reasoning: Compare an unexpected answer with authoritative data, resolver configuration and subsequent connections. Review query patterns in context without decoding or publishing sensitive content.
evidence: DNSSEC authenticates covered DNS data when validation succeeds; it does not encrypt queries or make a destination benign. Encrypted DNS protects a transport path but does not solve endpoint compromise.
defense: Protect resolver and zone administration, validate where appropriate, enforce necessary egress policy and correlate DNS with host evidence. Retest legitimate split-horizon behavior.

title: Lateral movement and remote-management abuse
mechanism: Lateral movement uses reachable services and sufficient credentials or vulnerabilities to act on another system. Legitimate administration tools can be used for legitimate or unauthorized activity.
prerequisites: A path requires source access, destination reachability, accepted identity and permission for the desired operation. A tunnel can alter reachability without creating application authorization.
reasoning: Draw each hop with its account, service and permitted operation. Identify where shared credentials or broad administrative groups make the path wider than intended.
evidence: A remote-management process or SSH session alone is not malicious. Compare account, target, time and action against approved activity.
defense: Reduce shared privilege, restrict management sources, isolate service accounts and record remote actions. Test account revocation and existing-session termination separately.

title: Denial of service: resource models
mechanism: Availability attacks can exhaust bandwidth, connection state, CPU, memory or application work queues. Reflection and amplification depend on third-party behavior and often forged source addresses.
prerequisites: Identify the limiting resource and the legitimate service requirement. A high-volume test can create operational harm without proving a useful repair.
reasoning: Use an offline resource model or documented counters to explain arrival rate, service rate and capacity. Plan any real capacity test as a separate controlled performance exercise.
evidence: A timeout does not locate the bottleneck. One service failure may result from an upstream dependency, client limit or measurement artifact.
defense: Constrain exposed services, apply source validation and suitable rate/capacity controls, and plan upstream protection where required. Avoid treating a successful flood as a necessary demonstration.

title: Wireless impersonation and enrollment trust
mechanism: A copied network name can resemble a trusted wireless network without establishing the same identity. Management and enrollment weaknesses can expose traffic or availability.
prerequisites: Client selection, authentication mode, certificate validation and proximity determine the relevant conditions. A visible duplicate name is not enough to establish successful impersonation.
reasoning: Review which identity a client verifies and how it chooses a network. Compare approved onboarding with a configuration that lacks the intended validation in a dedicated lab.
evidence: Radio interference and roaming can resemble disruption. Protected management features do not replace proper authentication or segmentation.
defense: Use appropriate enterprise validation or protected credentials, controlled provisioning, guest isolation and monitoring. Do not run disruption or deauthentication tests on shared radio space.

title: Detection engineering and false positives
mechanism: A detection maps observations to a hypothesis. It should state required data, expected signal, alternative explanations and a validation procedure.
prerequisites: Define which packets, switch logs, authentication events or endpoint records are needed and verify collection actually works. Use synthetic fixtures with known outcomes.
reasoning: Correlate a configuration anomaly with the affected connection and action. Add a negative control such as legitimate gateway failover, administrative maintenance or user password mistakes.
evidence: Technique labels are not verdicts. Absence of alerts may mean missing telemetry, not absence of activity; several tools can reflect the same underlying event.
defense: Measure coverage and false positives, document blind spots and preserve evidence. Retest after control changes and validate permitted activity still works.

title: Tools: observe, model and validate
mechanism: Choose a tool by the question: packet meaning, route state, service identity, policy decision or endpoint behavior. Its output must be interpreted within that scope.
prerequisites: Use approved captures and synthetic logs first. Distinguish offline parsing from active discovery, packet generation, poisoning and credential operations.
reasoning: Wireshark/TShark inspect evidence; Nmap checks selected reachable services; Scapy can parse saved packets or generate traffic, which are different activities. Match the tool mode to the exercise.
evidence: Responder, Bettercap and Impacket include capabilities that can alter network behavior or interact with authentication. Naming a tool does not establish that every mode is suitable for a given lab.
defense: Use a separately scoped isolated environment for active validation, record versions and exact behavior, and restore it afterward. This addition provides offline analysis commands and tabletop exercises.
